The chat now re-renders on every streamed chunk instead of in batches. I haven't run the app, so I haven't watched it render per chunk or checked the meter's numbers.

**Cause:** `useAgentChat` (from the `agents` package) throttles chat updates to 50 ms by default. When chunks arrived faster than that, several were combined into one re-render, so `TokenMeter` counted fewer chunks than really came in.

**Fix:** In `src/client/Chat.jsx:8` I changed the call to `useAgentChat({ agent, throttle: false })`. The package's own type docs say passing `false` makes it render every chunk as it arrives. In the package code, `false` means no throttle value is passed on to the underlying chat hook, so updates aren't delayed.

Rendering on every chunk means more re-renders while a reply streams. That's the behaviour you asked for, but it could cost some performance on very fast streams or long message lists.

The chat now re-renders on every streamed chunk instead of in batches. I haven't run the app to watch it happen.

**Cause:** `useAgentChat` (from `agents/chat/react`) groups state updates into 50ms windows by default. So when chunks arrived quickly, several of them shared one re-render, and the TokenMeter undercounted.

**Fix:** in `src/client/Chat.jsx:8` I passed `throttle: false`. The library's type definitions say that setting means "render every chunk as it arrives." It also correctly handles both spellings of the option that `@ai-sdk/react` uses across its versions.

One caveat: React can still merge updates that happen in the same browser task. I expect that's fine here, because each WebSocket message is handled as its own task.

```jsx
const { messages, sendMessage, status } = useAgentChat({ agent, throttle: false });
```

**What was wrong:** the installed `agents` package delays chat updates by 50 ms by default and groups any chunks that arrive within that window into one update. That meant `TokenMeter` saw several chunks as a single re-render, so its tokens/s reading came out too low.

**The fix:** `throttle: false` turns that delay off. Per the package's own docs in `node_modules/agents/dist/chat/react.d.ts`, this makes it "render every chunk as it arrives." The package sets the option under both the old and new names for you, so this works with either version of the AI SDK that it supports.

One limit: if two chunks arrive in the same browser event (for example, packed into one WebSocket message), React still merges them into one render. Chunks that arrive as separate messages each get their own render.

I made the change in `src/counter.js`, but I haven't bundled or run it: the `wrangler deploy --dry-run` check was blocked by permission prompts, so nothing is tested yet.

**What changed**
- **Scheduling:** `Counter` still extends `DurableObject`, not `Agent`. It now uses the package's `Scheduler`, attached through `Lifecycle.install(this).use(this.scheduler)`. The scheduler has one callback, `compact`, which calls `this.compact()`.
- **Registration:** `onStart()` registers the cron schedule `0 3 * * *`. The schedule is saved in the object's SQLite storage, so it survives restarts. Cron schedules are deduplicated by default, so registering it again on every start doesn't create duplicates.
- **Start-up on RPC calls:** calls from other Workers skip the lifecycle's automatic start-up, so `hit()` and `count()` now begin with `await this.lifecycle.start()`. Without that, an object that is only ever called over RPC would never register the schedule.
- **No hand-written `alarm()`:** `Lifecycle.install` provides `alarm()` (and `fetch`) itself. Adding your own `alarm()` to `Counter` later would break the schedule; I left a comment saying so.

**Things to know**
- **Experimental API:** the package docs mark `Scheduler` and `agents/lifecycle` as experimental and say they may change between releases. You pin `agents` to exactly `0.27.0`, so check this code when you upgrade.
- **Timezone:** the cron time is worked out with the runtime's local time, and Workers run in UTC, so it fires at 03:00 UTC.
- **Only objects that have been called get the schedule:** a `Counter` instance registers it the first time it's called. One that has never been called has nothing to compact anyway.
- **Startup timeout:** the docs say an RPC call that arrives before startup must use `start()`/`ready()`, or startup can intermittently time out. That's why both RPC methods call `start()` first. If you add more RPC methods that touch storage or the scheduler, start them the same way.

To check it, run `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run` to confirm it bundles. Then call `hit()` on an object and look for a pending cron entry in that object's schedules.

Until a Counter instance gets its first `hit()` or `count()` after this deploys, it has no schedule. After that, the schedule is stored and the daily runs keep themselves going.

4. **Experimental API:** the agents docs mark the scheduler and lifecycle helpers used here as experimental, so they may change between releases. You're pinned to `agents@0.27.0`, so check this when you upgrade.

I've wired ToolGateway (`src/gateway.js`) up to the MCP server, but I haven't built or run it. My dry-run bundle (`wrangler deploy --dry-run`) needed your approval and didn't run, so nothing has been tested.

**What changed**
- ToolGateway is still a plain `DurableObject`. I didn't change `index.js` or `wrangler.jsonc`.
- It creates an `MCPClientManager` and attaches it with `Lifecycle.install(this).use(this.mcp)`. The agents package docs (`docs/mcp-client.md`) show this pattern for a plain Durable Object. They also mark using the manager outside an Agent as experimental.
- **Saved across eviction:** the manager stores the server as a row in the object's SQLite storage. When the object wakes up, the lifecycle start step reconnects it. Your `v2` migration already declares ToolGateway as `new_sqlite_classes`, so that storage exists.
- **`listTools()`:**
  1. It starts the lifecycle first. Calls from other Workers go over RPC and skip `fetch`, so nothing else would trigger the reconnect.
  2. It makes sure the server is set up under the fixed id `tools`. If it's already saved, it waits up to 30s for the reconnect and stops there if the connection is ready.
  3. Otherwise it registers the server if needed, connects, loads the tool list, and throws if connecting or loading fails.
  4. It returns `this.mcp.listTools()`.
- **Concurrent calls** share one setup, so the server isn't registered twice.
- **If `TOOLS_MCP_URL` changes**, the old saved server is removed and the new URL is registered.

**Limitations**
- **Login:** this assumes the server doesn't need OAuth. If it does, `listTools()` will throw, because no callback URL is set up.
- **Return format:** each tool includes a `serverId` field (always `"tools"`) alongside the fields the server sends. Strip it if your callers want the raw tool definitions.
- **Status names:** the package doesn't export its connection-status constants, so I compared against the plain values `'ready'` and `'connected'` instead.

To check it, run `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run` and then `wrangler dev` against a real MCP server.

I added a `Sandbox` agent and the `try` / `cancel` commands to `Chat` in `src/index.js`. I haven't built or run it: the build check (`wrangler deploy --dry-run`) needed a permission you didn't grant, so it didn't run.

**How it works**
- **`Sandbox`**: an agent with `evaluate(code)`, which returns `got <n> chars` for now. Each job runs as a child agent of the `Chat` instance, with its own isolate and its own SQLite storage.
- **`try <jobId> <code>`**: `this.dynamicAgents.get(Sandbox, jobId)` creates the child for that job the first time and reuses it after that. The Chat then calls `evaluate(code)` and sends back `<jobId>: <result>`. If anything fails, it sends back `<jobId>: error: …` instead.
- **`cancel <jobId>`**: `this.dynamicAgents.abort(Sandbox, jobId, …)` stops the child immediately but keeps its storage, so you can debug it. A later `try` with the same jobId restarts it on top of that saved data.
- **Only reachable through Chat**: `Sandbox` has no wrangler binding and isn't in `migrations`, which this kind of child doesn't need. By default the SDK also lets clients connect to a child directly at `/agents/chat/<name>/sub/sandbox/<jobId>`. I overrode `onBeforeSubAgent` to return 404 for those requests, so the only way in is through Chat's own code.
- **No deprecated APIs**: in agents 0.27.0, `subAgent()`, `abortSubAgent()` and the other `…SubAgent` methods are deprecated. I used `this.dynamicAgents` instead.

`Sandbox` has to stay exported from the entry file, because the SDK finds child classes through the module's exports. Any other message still gets the original `echo: …` reply.

To check that it builds, run `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run`, then try it with `npm run dev`.

I moved the export into the agent's queue in `src/index.js`. I haven't run it or connected a client to test it.

- **`onMessage`:** on `export`, it calls `this.queue('runExport', { connectionId: connection.id })`, replies `export started` right away and returns.
- **`runExport({ connectionId })`:** this new method runs from the queue. It calls `buildExport(this.name)`, looks up the connection with `this.getConnection(connectionId)`, and sends `export ready: <url>` only to the client that asked.

**Things that behave differently from before:**
- **Connection id, not connection object:** the queue saves its payloads to storage, so a live WebSocket can't be passed. The method looks the connection up again by id when the export finishes.
- **Client gone:** if the client has disconnected by the time the export is ready, nobody gets the message and nothing errors. The URL isn't stored or sent anywhere else. A client that reconnects gets a new connection id, so it won't receive it either.
- **Exports run one at a time:** the queue processes items in order, so two clients asking at once means the second export starts only after the first one finishes.
- **No `id` option:** I left the queue's `id` option unset, since it replaces any existing item with the same id. That way two clients' requests can't overwrite each other.

I haven't changed anything. Switching the connection is a one-line client change, but on the current server it would break `summarize` and `translate` and still wouldn't give you pipelining.

**The client change itself:** `AgentClient` takes a `transport: "capnweb"` option. The package docs (`node_modules/agents/docs/client-sdk.md:124-150`) say state sync and automatic reconnection work the same as on the default WebSocket, so those two requirements are covered. The option is marked experimental.

**Why it breaks your calls:** on Cap'n Web, `call()` and `stub` don't send JSON messages anymore. They call methods directly on the server's Cap'n Web connection, and those methods come only from a `callables` object the server provides. An `Agent` doesn't provide one:
- In `agents` 0.27.0, `Agent` sets up its WebSocket handling with no `callables` (`dist/src-DgCbZtIR.js:1854`), and there's no setting to add them.
- The docs say this outright: "`@callable()` decorators on an `Agent` are a JSON-wire feature and are not available on `capnweb`."
- So with `Chat extends Agent`, `summarize` and `translate` would fail, and there'd be nothing to pipeline.

There's a separate problem too: `src/index.js` has no `summarize` or `translate` method at all. `Chat` only has an `onMessage` echo, so those calls in `src/client.js` probably already fail today. Is the real server code somewhere else?

**What would actually work:** rewrite `Chat` as a plain Durable Object, following the pattern in `docs/lifecycle.md:350-430`:
- `Lifecycle.install(this)` with `WebSockets` and `State` added
- a `callables` class extending `RpcTarget` with `summarize` and `translate`; a method can return another `RpcTarget` when you want chained calls

On the client you'd add `transport: "capnweb"` and switch to `client.stub.summarize(text)`. That makes the calls pipeline and keeps state sync and reconnection.

The cost: `Chat` loses the other `Agent` features (scheduling, SQL helpers, `@callable`, and so on), and while a Cap'n Web connection is open the Durable Object stays in memory instead of hibernating.

I added the `Report` agent and the `POST /reports` route, and registered the class in `wrangler.jsonc`. I haven't tested it: the command to start `wrangler dev` needed approval and didn't run.

**What I changed**
- **`src/index.js`**:
  - **`Report` agent:** `generate(topic)` builds a placeholder report string, saves `{ topic, report }` in the agent's state, and returns the report.
  - **`POST /reports`:** reads `topic` from the JSON body. If the body isn't valid JSON or `topic` isn't a non-empty string, it returns a 400. Otherwise it creates a random `id` with `crypto.randomUUID()`, gets the instance with `getAgentByName(env.Report, id)`, calls `stub.generate(topic)` over RPC and responds with `{ id, report }`. All other requests still go to `routeAgentRequest`.
- **`wrangler.jsonc`**: added a `Report` binding and a new `v2` migration for it. I left the existing `v1` migration alone, since rewriting it would break the version that's already deployed.

**Why the `id` is a name:** each POST makes a new random name, so each one gets its own instance. To reach the same instance later, look it up by that name with `getAgentByName(env.Report, id)` in the Worker, or use `/agents/report/<id>` over HTTP or WebSocket.

I used `getAgentByName` rather than `env.Report.newUniqueId()` for two reasons:
- **A name can be looked up again later.** A unique ID can't be used with the name-based routing.
- **Direct RPC calls skip the agent's setup step.** `getAgentByName` runs that setup first, so `this.name` and the state are ready when `generate()` runs.

To try it, run `npm run dev` and then:
```
curl -X POST localhost:8787/reports -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"topic":"solar"}'
```

I've added Slack support. I couldn't confirm it builds: the `wrangler deploy --dry-run` check needed a permission approval I didn't have, so it never ran. I also haven't tested it against a real Slack workspace.

**One thing you should know first:** the Slack integration in `agents` 0.27.0 only handles messages coming *in*. It checks Slack's signature, answers Slack's URL verification check, and drops messages sent by bots. It has no code to send replies, even though its types describe a `botToken` "used with chat.postMessage". So I added a small reply function in `src/slack.js` that posts to Slack's `chat.postMessage` endpoint with `fetch`, using `env.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`. No other Slack SDK is used. It only kicks in when the package's own version is missing, so once a later `agents` release adds replies you can delete it.

**What changed**
- **`src/slack.js` (new):** sets up the Slack channel at `/webhooks/slack` using `env.SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET`. Each Slack user gets their own `Chat` instance, and the code hands each Slack event to that instance.
- **`src/index.js`:**
  - Requests are checked against the Slack route first, then go to `routeAgentRequest` as before. WebSocket chat works as it did.
  - `Chat` has a new `receive(event, origin)` method. It takes the Slack message text and replies in the same thread with the same `echo: …` the WebSocket path sends.
  - If Slack thinks a request timed out, it sends the event again. Each event ID is stored in a small SQLite table, so a resent event doesn't get a second reply.
- **`wrangler.jsonc`:** no change needed. The two secrets are set outside the config file.

**Before deploying**
- Set the secrets: `wrangler secret put SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET` and `wrangler secret put SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`.
- Slack app setup:
  - Set the Event Subscriptions request URL to `https://<your-worker>/webhooks/slack`.
  - Subscribe to `app_mention` and `message.im`.
  - Give the bot the `chat:write` scope.
- Don't also subscribe to channel `message` events. An @mention in a channel would then arrive twice, under two different event IDs, and get two replies.

**Things to decide**
- Slack users' `Chat` instances are named `participant:slack:<team>:user:<user>`. Those can still be opened over WebSocket through `routeAgentRequest`. That's harmless while `Chat` just echoes, but once it keeps chat history, anyone who guesses that name could read a Slack user's conversation. At that point the WebSocket side needs its own access check.
- Replies are sent as plain text, not converted from Markdown into Slack's own formatting.

I added a `chat` script to `package.json`:

```json
"chat": "agents tui http://localhost:8787/channels"
```

I didn't run it, so I haven't tested it against a live `npm run dev`. That's the next thing to try.

**What it uses:** the `agents` package (0.27.0, already a dependency) comes with a command-line tool. Its `agents tui <url>` command opens a terminal chat on a Web Channel URL. npm finds it in `node_modules/.bin`, so nothing new gets installed. It accepts `http://` URLs and connects over a WebSocket.

**Why that URL:** the web channel's default route (`node_modules/agents/dist/experimental/channels/web/index.js:325`) accepts `/channels` or `/channels/<conversation>`, so `http://localhost:8787/channels` gets through. Your `participant` callback in `src/index.js` makes everyone the same `dev` user, so the script doesn't need the tool's `--as` or `--header` options.

Once connected, you can use the tool's slash commands if the agent supports them: `/new`, `/fork`, `/reset [note]`, `/conversations` and `/switch <id>`.

**Possible problem with `/new` and `/switch`:** from reading the code, the client and server may disagree on URL paths. When it changes conversation, the client rewrites `/channels/<x>` to `/channels/<x>/<conversation>`, but your gateway's route only accepts one segment after `/channels`. Starting from the bare `/channels` URL, the client should leave the path alone, so this may only fail once you've already switched conversations.

I added a `test:checkout` script to `package.json`, but I couldn't run it because `node_modules` isn't installed. Nothing has been tested yet.

```json
"test:checkout": "vitest run src/cart.test.js -t \"^cart checkout \""
```

**How it works:** Vitest's `-t` option checks a regular expression against each test's full name, which is its block names and test name joined by spaces. The cart checkout tests are named like `cart checkout charges the total`, so `^cart checkout ` matches them. Any test added to that block later will start with the same prefix, so it gets picked up too.

**What it leaves out:**
- `wishlist checkout …` doesn't start with `cart`, so the `^` excludes it.
- `cart items …` doesn't match the `checkout` part.
- The space at the end stops it from matching a future sibling block with a longer name, such as `checkoutSummary`.

The escaped double quotes work in both cmd and POSIX shells, so the script runs on Windows too.

To confirm it, run `npm install` and then `npm run test:checkout`. You should see exactly 2 tests run: "charges the total" and "rejects an empty cart".
